Checklist Item: Indicate Mendelian randomization (MR) as the study's design in the title and/or the abstract if that is a main purpose of the study
Response: Title explicitly states "triangulation framework" and MR context; Abstract describes 5-dimension MR-based framework with all key MR methods (UVMR, MVMR, LDSC, coloc, CAUSE, MRlap).

Checklist Item: Explain the scientific background and rationale for the reported study. What is the exposure? Is a potential causal relationship between exposure and outcome plausible? Justify why MR is a helpful method to address the study question.
Response: Exposure: insomnia (UKB, n=462,341). Outcome: Alzheimer's disease (IGAP Kunkle, n=63,926). Rationale: numerous published MR studies claim insomnia→AD causal, but LD-clump sensitivity is systematically omitted. MR is justified because RCTs randomizing insomnia are infeasible, and GWAS-identified genetic instruments provide a natural experiment. Historical analogy to GWAS candidate-gene era (Introduction ¶1) justifies the need for methodological standardization.

Checklist Item: State specific objectives clearly, including pre-specified causal hypotheses (if any). State that MR is a method that, under specific assumptions, intends to estimate causal effects.
Response: Objective: propose and validate a 5-dimension triangulation framework for comorbidity MR, then apply it to insomnia–AD as proof-of-concept. Pre-registered hypothesis (OSF): insomnia as causal upstream of AD. No prior commitment to causal direction in analysis; framework is designed to detect both causal and non-causal architectures. MR assumptions (relevance, independence, exclusion restriction) are stated in Methods ¶1.

Checklist Item: Describe the study design and the underlying population. Describe the setting, locations, and relevant dates, including periods of recruitment, exposure, follow-up, and data collection.
Response: All GWAS are publicly available summary statistics from IEU OpenGWAS and NIAGADS. Populations: European (UKB, IGAP, Bellenguez) and East Asian (GARD, Chen/Kim/Lam 2024). Recruitment periods: UKB 2006–2010; IGAP meta-analysis (pre-2019); Bellenguez 2022; INTERVAL 2012–2014. No individual-level data were accessed; all analyses are two-sample summary-level MR.

Checklist Item: Give the eligibility criteria, and the sources and methods of selection of participants. Report the sample size, and whether any power or sample size calculations were carried out prior to the main analysis.
Location in Manuscript: Methods — Data sources table; Results Dimension 1
Response: Insomnia: ukb-b-3957 (n=462,341 EUR). AD primary: ieu-b-2 Kunkle (n=63,926, 21,982 cases). AD replication: Bellenguez (n=487,511, 85,934 cases). Education: ieu-a-1239 (n=117,487). EA replication: GCST90296498 (n=165,232 EAS) + GARD/NG00182 (n=6,518 EAS). Post-hoc power calculation reported in Results Dimension 1 Summary: clumped UVMR has ~7% power at β=0.10.

Checklist Item: Describe measurement, quality control and selection of genetic variants.
Response: Instruments selected at P<5e-8 genome-wide significance. LD-clumping at r²<0.001, window 10Mb (loose) and 5Mb (tight). HM3 SNP list used for LD reference. Instrument counts: unclumped=2,462; loose=54; tight=37. Instrument sensitivity summarized in Supplementary Table S2 (method, instrument set, n_SNPs, β, SE, P). Mean F-statistic for clumped insomnia instruments: 39.8.

Checklist Item: For each exposure, outcome, and other relevant variables, describe methods of assessment and diagnostic criteria for diseases.
Response: Insomnia: self-reported frequency (UKB field 1200). AD: clinically diagnosed (IGAP criteria: NINCDS-ADRDA; Bellenguez: clinical + proxy). Educational attainment: college completion (Lee 2018) and years of education (Chen 2024). Proteins: INTERVAL aptamer-based SOMAscan (Sun 2018). Metabolites: Nightingale NMR metabolomics (Kettunen 2016). PD: clinically diagnosed (Nalls 2019). MS: clinically diagnosed (IMSGC 2019).

Checklist Item: Provide details of ethics committee approval and participant informed consent, if relevant.
Response: All GWAS data are publicly available summary statistics from studies with existing ethical approvals: UKB (North West Multi-centre Research Ethics Committee, 11/NW/0382); IGAP (institutional ethics per participating cohort); INTERVAL (National Research Ethics Service, 11/EE/0538). No new data collection was performed.

Checklist Item: Explicitly state the three core IV assumptions for the main analysis (relevance, independence and exclusion restriction) as well assumptions for any additional or sensitivity analysis.
Response: Core IV assumptions: (1) Relevance: instruments are strongly associated with exposure (P<5e-8, mean F=39.8); (2) Independence: LD-clumping (r²<0.001) to ensure instrument independence, with clumped-vs-unclumped comparison as sensitivity; (3) Exclusion restriction: assessed via MR-Egger intercept, MR-PRESSO, CAUSE (which partitions correlated pleiotropy), and MRlap (which corrects for sample overlap). MVMR further adjusts for measured confounders (depression, LDL-C, educational attainment).

Checklist Item: Describe how quantitative variables were handled in the analyses (i.e., scale, units, model).
Response: All exposures and outcomes analyzed as continuous traits on the log-odds scale for binary outcomes (AD, PD, MS). Betas reported as log-odds ratio per 1-unit change in exposure. IVs weighted by inverse-variance of SNP-outcome association.

Checklist Item: Describe how genetic variants were handled in the analyses and, if applicable, how their weights were selected.
Response: Harmonized to align effect alleles between exposure and outcome; palindromic SNPs with ambiguous alleles resolved using effect allele frequency. IVs weighted by 1/SE²(outcome). Harmonization via TwoSampleMR::harmonise_data() with default action=2 (palindromic SNPs excluded if EAF unavailable).

Checklist Item: Describe the MR estimator (e.g. two-stage least squares, Wald ratio) and related statistics. Detail the included covariates and, in case of two-sample MR, whether the same covariate set was used for adjustment in the two samples.
Response: Primary estimator: IVW (fixed-effects, multiplicative random-effects if heterogeneity detected). Sensitivity estimators: MR-Egger (with SIMEX correction where applicable), weighted median, weighted mode. CAUSE: Bayesian mixture model (v1.2.2). MRlap: overlap-corrected MR (v0.0.3.1). MVMR: multivariable IVW. Two-step mediation: product-of-coefficients with delta-method SE and bootstrap CI. Two-sample MR design; covariate adjustment was GWAS-specific (UKB: age, sex, 10 PCs; IGAP: age, sex, 5 PCs; INTERVAL: age, sex, 10 PCs, plate).

Checklist Item: Explain how missing data were addressed.
Response: Summary-level data: SNPs not present in outcome GWAS were excluded during harmonization. SNPs with missing N were excluded. For HDL.run, missing N filled with median. No individual-level missing data imputation was performed (summary statistics preclude this).

Checklist Item: If applicable, indicate how multiple testing was addressed.
Response: Protein mediation (25 evaluable): Benjamini-Hochberg FDR (q<0.05 threshold). Metabolite mediation (10 metabolites): BH-FDR. PheWAS (4 outcomes x 4 methods): nominal significance with heterogeneity assessment. All other analyses: nominal α=0.05 with explicit caveats for borderline results (CAUSE P=0.039 noted as borderline).

Checklist Item: Describe any methods or prior knowledge used to assess the assumptions or justify their validity.
Response: Relevance: F-statistics reported. Independence: clumped-vs-unclumped sensitivity; MR-Egger intercept test for directional pleiotropy; Cochran's Q for heterogeneity; leave-one-out analysis; MR-PRESSO global test. Exclusion restriction: CAUSE partitions causal from correlated-pleiotropy effects; MRlap corrects for sample overlap; MVMR controls for measured confounders. Coloc PP.H4 assesses shared-vs-distinct causal variants. Steiger tests direction of effect.

Checklist Item: Describe any sensitivity analyses or additional analyses performed (e.g. comparison of effect estimates from different approaches, independent replication, bias analytic techniques, validation of instruments, simulations).
Response: (1) LD-clumping parameter variation (loose vs tight). (2) Chromosome-19 exclusion (LDSC no-chr19, UVMR no-chr19). (3) Exposure substitution (education→protein→AD as alternative to insomnia→protein→AD). (4) Bellenguez replication for AD outcome. (5) East Asian cross-ancestry replication of education→AD. (6) UKB-PPP published pQTL verification (Sun 2023 ST9/10). (7) Bootstrap CI (5,000 resamples) for mediation. (8) CAUSE on LD-pruned variant set (1,645 variants) vs full clumped set. (9) No formal simulation study was performed.

Checklist Item: Name statistical software and package(s), including version and settings used.
Response: R v4.5.2. Packages: TwoSampleMR (v0.6.8), coloc (v5.2.3), MRlap (v0.0.3.1), cause (v1.2.2), MVMR (v0.4), ieugwasr (v1.0.0), susieR (v0.14.2). Python v3.13: numpy, scipy, pandas, matplotlib, seaborn. LDSC v1.0.1 with pre-computed EUR LD Scores. All settings are recorded in reproducible scripts at [GitHub URL].

Checklist Item: State whether the study protocol and details were pre-registered (as well as when and where).
Response: Pre-registered at OSF ([OSF registration link]). The original pre-registered hypothesis posited insomnia as a causal upstream of AD. The study was conducted transparently: the framework's gatekeeper dimension (LD-clump sensitivity) immediately revealed signal instability, and the revised conclusion was reached through multi-method triangulation rather than adherence to the pre-registered hypothesis.

Checklist Item: Report the numbers of individuals at each stage of included studies and reasons for exclusion. Consider use of a flow diagram.
Response: Fig. 1 provides a pipeline flow diagram of the 5-dimension framework. Instrument counts per dimension: unclumped UVMR (2,462 SNPs) → clumped (54 loose/37 tight) → CAUSE (1,645 LD-pruned) → MRlap (40) → MVMR (44/29). Protein screen: 36 targeted → 25 evaluable → 11 excluded (Step2<2 instruments). Replication: Bellenguez (variable per analysis). EA replication: 100 instruments → 9 harmonized.

Checklist Item: Report summary statistics for phenotypic exposure(s), outcome(s), and other relevant variables (e.g. means, SDs, proportions).
Response: Insomnia: prevalence ~10% (UKB). AD: prevalence ~1-2% (UKB-age population); Kunkle ncase=21,982 (34.4%); Bellenguez ncase=85,934 (17.6%). SNP heritability (LDSC): h²_insomnia=0.059 (SE=0.003); h²_AD=0.060 (SE=0.009). Summary-level GWAS data; individual-level phenotypic distributions are not available.

Checklist Item: If the data sources include meta-analyses of previous studies, provide the assessments of heterogeneity across these studies.
Response: Bellenguez AD GWAS meta-analysis showed extreme heterogeneity when used with education instruments (Cochran's Q P=1.7e-11). This dataset was therefore used for replication (coloc) only, not for primary causal estimation. Bellenguez CAUSE replication (P=0.002) was accompanied by this extreme heterogeneity and interpreted with caution.

Checklist Item: For two-sample MR: (i) Provide justification of the similarity of the genetic variant-exposure associations between the exposure and outcome samples. (ii) Provide information on the number of individuals who overlap between the exposure and outcome studies.
Response: All MR analyses are two-sample. Overlap between insomnia GWAS (UKB) and AD GWAS (IGAP, independent cohort) is zero. Some overlap between insomnia (UKB) and Bellenguez AD (UKB subset). MRlap explicitly models and corrects for sample overlap (corrected β=−0.078, P=0.43). Intercept from MR-Egger additionally reported to assess residual bias.

Checklist Item: Report the associations between genetic variant and exposure, and between genetic variant and outcome, preferably on an interpretable scale.
Response: Reported in text as β (log-OR) with SE. Unclumped IVW: β=+0.104, SE=0.031 per log-OR of AD per unit increase in insomnia genetic risk. Clumped IVW: β=−0.130, SE=0.203. Supplementary Figure 2 displays the forest plot of all MR estimates. Scatter plot available in archived analysis outputs.

Checklist Item: Report MR estimates of the relationship between exposure and outcome, and the measures of uncertainty from the MR analysis, on an interpretable scale, such as odds ratio or relative risk per SD difference.
Response: All estimates reported as β (log-OR) with SE, P-value. Convertible to OR = exp(β). Key estimates: unclumped UVMR OR≈1.11 (P=0.0009); clumped UVMR OR≈0.88 (P=0.52); MRlap corrected OR≈0.92 (P=0.43); MVMR education OR≈0.27 per unit (P=0.008); PheWAS AD OR≈0.72 (P=1.1e-5); PheWAS PD OR≈0.68 (P=7.2e-6).

Checklist Item: If relevant, consider translating estimates of relative risk into absolute risk for a meaningful time period.
Response: Absolute risk translation was not performed. The analyses estimate causal effects in log-odds scale; conversion to absolute risk would require baseline AD incidence rates and is beyond the scope of the present genetic epidemiological study.

Checklist Item: Consider plots to visualize results (e.g. forest plot, scatterplot of associations between genetic variants and outcome versus between genetic variants and exposure).
Response: Fig. 2: MR forest plot of bidirectional estimates across methods. Fig. 3: Protein and metabolite mediation forest plots and volcano plots. Fig. 4: Education PheWAS forest plot. Fig. 5: Framework quadrant classification diagram. Supplementary Fig. 3C: G2b volcano and top-15 forest plot.

Checklist Item: Report the assessment of the validity of the assumptions.
Response: MR-Egger intercept: highly significant for reverse direction (AD→insomnia), consistent with horizontal pleiotropy. Cochran's Q: significant heterogeneity across several analyses (noted where applicable). Leave-one-out: no single SNP drove the results (archived in analysis outputs). CAUSE: partitions pleiotropy; forward signal borderline (P=0.039). CAUSE elpd Z-score=2.07 (Kunkle).

Checklist Item: Report any additional statistics (e.g., assessments of heterogeneity across genetic variants, such as I², Q statistic or E-value).
Response: Cochran's Q reported for primary MR analyses. Bellenguez dataset heterogeneity flagged (Q P=1.7e-11) and interpretation accordingly downgraded. Mean F-statistic for clumped insomnia instruments: 39.8. Conditional F-statistics for MVMR computed but not reported in the main text (available in Supplementary Table S3). E-value was not computed.

Checklist Item: Report any sensitivity analyses to assess the robustness of the main results to violations of the assumptions.
Response: Clumping parameter sensitivity: loose (r²<0.001, 10Mb) vs tight (r²<0.001, 5Mb). Chromosome-19 exclusion: LDSC no-chr19, UVMR unclumped no-chr19. Exposure substitution: education as alternative exposure for protein mediation. Bellenguez replication. MVMR with and without chr19. All sensitivity results: see Supplementary Tables S2, S3.

Checklist Item: Report results from other sensitivity analyses or additional analyses.
Response: MR-Egger, weighted median, weighted mode for PheWAS. Bootstrap CI for mediation (5,000 resamples). MR-PRESSO excluded for individual-level outlier diagnosis (summary data insufficient). UKB-PPP NEFL/GFAP targeted verification (reported as infeasible: NEFL zero cis-pQTL, GFAP single instrument null).

Checklist Item: Report any assessment of direction of causal relationship (e.g., bidirectional MR).
Response: Bidirectional MR: forward (insomnia→AD) and reverse (AD→insomnia) performed for all method families. Reverse direction consistently null-to-tiny with significant Egger intercept. Steiger testing: direction ambiguous; r_from_lor→AD→insomnia; p→r→insomnia→AD. Median r≈0.002 per SNP. Steiger not relied upon for directionality determination.

Checklist Item: When relevant, report and compare with estimates from non-MR analyses.
Response: Non-MR (observational) estimates were not directly compared. The Introduction and Discussion reference the observational literature on insomnia–AD comorbidity, but formal comparison with observational effect sizes was not a study objective.

Checklist Item: Consider additional plots to visualize results (e.g., leave-one-out analyses).
Response: Leave-one-out plots available in archived analysis outputs. Supplementary Figure 3A/B: CRP/IL-6 mediation forest plots. Supplementary Figure 3C: G2b volcano and top-15 forest plot. Fig. 5: Framework synthesis quadrant diagram.

Checklist Item: Summarize key results with reference to study objectives.
Response: Key result: unclumped insomnia→AD MR signal (+0.10, P=9.3e-4) is a replication of published literature but does not survive LD-clumping (P=0.52-0.64). 3 of 4 causal methods converge to null. Comorbidity is APOE-locus-specific shared liability, not genome-wide genetic correlation. Education is a cross-ancestry protective factor partially mediated by triglycerides (~9%). Framework classifies insomnia–AD as quadrant III (shared liability, no independent causal upstream).

Checklist Item: Discuss limitations of the study, taking into account the validity of the IV assumptions, other sources of potential bias, and imprecision.
Response: Seven limitations explicitly discussed: (1) framework requires adequately powered GWAS; (2) residual LD at unmeasured variants possible despite clumping; (3) plasma proteome may not reflect brain proteome; (4) EA replication underpowered; (5) multi-state time-to-event modeling not performed; (6) CAUSE borderline P=0.039 discordant with other methods; (7) primarily European-ancestry. Additional boundaries: low clumped UVMR power (~7% at β=0.10); protein-mediation null is instrument-strength-limited. UKB-PPP full-summary re-evaluation warranted.

Checklist Item: Interpretation consistent with results, taking into account IV assumptions and other relevant evidence.
Response: Interpretation consistently notes that triangulation converges on shared liability. CAUSE borderline result (P=0.039) is explicitly acknowledged as a methodological divergence, not dismissed, and interpreted as a "non-null remainder" warranting future investigation. The counter-argument (clumped null may reflect low power, not absent causality) is addressed via MRlap convergent evidence.

Checklist Item: Discussion of possible mechanism and plausibility of the causal pathway.
Location in Manuscript: Discussion — Colocalization asymmetry; Null protein-mediation; Discussion — Central advance
Response: Mechanism: APOE ε4 is the shared causal variant (coloc reverse 18/32 loci, PP.H4 >0.98 at APOE region). Protein mediation null (25/25 evaluable, FDR=0) suggests plasma inflammation is not the genetically proxied mediator. TG mediation (indirect β=−0.031, q=5.7e-4) provides a lipid-mediated mechanism for education's protection. The protein-null/metabolite-positive dichotomy is discussed as a potentially informative architecture rather than a failure of detection.

Checklist Item: Discuss whether the results have clinical or public policy relevance, and to what extent they inform effect sizes of possible interventions.
Response: Clinical relevance: (1) insomnia→AD causal claim should not guide sleep-targeted AD prevention trials without instrument-quality verification; (2) educational attainment is a cross-ancestry protective factor; (3) TG-mediated pathway (~9% of education's effect) identifies lipid metabolism as a partially modifiable mediator. The triangulation framework (Box 1) provides standards for evaluating MR-based causal claims before they inform clinical or policy decisions.

Checklist Item: Discuss the generalizability of the study results (a) to other populations, (b) across other exposure periods/timings, and (c) across other levels of exposure.
Response: (a) EA replication showed directional consistency for education→AD; broader multi-ancestry generalizability is unconfirmed. (b) The study used lifetime insomnia liability (genetic instrument) and late-onset AD — period-specific effects (e.g., midlife vs late-life insomnia) could not be resolved. (c) Dose-response was not assessed (summary-level MR). (d) Framework generalizability to other comorbidity pairs (depression→CVD, RA→AD, T2D→PD) is proposed in Discussion as a direct extension.
